fatal_errors: The proposed 900 °C rapid-quench versus slow-cool intervention does not reconstruct the 1100–1300 °C water-quench temperature series and assumes that quenching after annealing will suppress ordering that may already have developed during the 900 °C hold.

The cited evidence concerns Fe–Mn–Ni–Cr–Al–Si and Ti–Nb–Cr–V–Ni–Al alloys rather than the target Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system, and it does not establish the claimed ordering-controlled FCC stability or property tradeoffs.

EBSD phase-fraction analysis alone generally cannot reliably distinguish chemically ordered B2 from disordered BCC because they share essentially the same lattice geometry; superlattice-sensitive diffraction or TEM is required.
explanation: The response identifies the important Ni–Al enrichment and B2 ordering motif and provides a nominally controlled, falsifiable comparison, so it captures part of the target mechanism. However, it misses the central temperature-dependent transformation pathway: cooling-induced miscibility-gap spinodal separation into reciprocal Ni–Al-rich and Co–Cr–Fe-rich BCC products, possible sequential decomposition, and subsequent B2 ordering. It also replaces the actual 1100–1300 °C water-quench comparison, 1100 °C baseline, and hardness/BCC-fraction trend with a speculative 900 °C cooling-rate experiment and unmeasured claims about cryogenic toughness and radiation tolerance. The supporting papers are compositionally remote and do not validate the proposed causal chain. Thus this is a partial mechanistic overlap rather than an evidence-supported reconstruction.
